clinicalPearls: An osteochondrosis (avascular necrosis) of a metatarsal head, most often the second metatarsal
It is the only osteochondrosis more common in females and typically presents in adolescence
Presents with forefoot pain, swelling and stiffness of the metatarsophalangeal joint, worse on weight bearing
Radiographs show flattening, sclerosis and later collapse and widening of the metatarsal head
Repetitive stress and the vulnerability of the metatarsal head blood supply are implicated
Early disease is managed conservatively with offloading; advanced disease with joint damage may need surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Freiberg disease is an osteochondrosis in which the subchondral bone of a metatarsal head (usually the second, the longest and most loaded) undergoes avascular necrosis. Repetitive microtrauma and mechanical overload, together with the tenuous blood supply of the metatarsal head, are thought to cause subchondral ischaemia, leading to bone collapse, articular surface flattening and fragmentation. Progressive joint incongruity results in pain, stiffness and secondary osteoarthritis of the metatarsophalangeal joint.
additionalInvestigations: MRI in early disease before radiographic change
Clinical assessment of the affected metatarsophalangeal joint
Exclusion of stress fracture and neuroma
Assessment of foot biomechanics and footwear
redFlags: Advanced joint collapse and secondary arthritis
Features suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis
reference.prognosis: Early disease often responds to conservative offloading with a good outcome, whereas advanced collapse can cause persistent pain and metatarsophalangeal arthritis requiring surgery.
pitfalls: Confusing it with a metatarsal stress fracture or Morton neuroma
Not imaging early forefoot pain with MRI when radiographs are normal
